it is called the Pillar of the Eagle's Cross; the people of knowledge told us so,

a: وهو من الدلفين في أصل الذنب
full.e: and it lies at the root of the Dolphin's tail, as you see it on the globes and in the books.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 8 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الدلفين: عشرة كواكب أربعة منها نيّرة تسمّى صليب الطائر، وتسمّيها العرب القَعود وهو البكر من الإبل الذي يُركب. وكوكب صغير نيّر تحتها هو عمود الصليب عند أصل ذنب الدلفين.

stories.title: القعود
stories.text: المعيّن الصغير في الدلفين هو «القعود» عند العرب، والقعود من الإبل ما يُقتعد أي يُركب. وهو اسم وصورة لا حكاية، من طريقة أهل البادية في ملء سمائهم بحيوانات حياتهم.

greek.seen: The dolphin who found Amphitrite.

stories.title: The matchmaking dolphin
stories.text: Poseidon wanted to marry the sea-nymph Amphitrite, but she fled and hid from him. A dolphin searched the seas, found her, and gently persuaded her to return. Poseidon married her and, in gratitude, placed the dolphin in the sky. Another story says it is the dolphin that rescued the poet Arion when sailors threw him overboard.
stories.source: Kitab al-Sama'; Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: الدلفين الذي وجد أمفيتريت.

stories.title: الدلفين الخاطب
stories.text: أراد بوسيدون الزواج من حورية البحر أمفيتريت فهربت واختبأت منه، فبحث دلفين في البحار حتى وجدها وأقنعها برفق بالعودة. فتزوّجها بوسيدون ورفع الدلفين إلى السماء شكرًا له. وتقول رواية أخرى إنه الدلفين الذي أنقذ الشاعر أريون حين ألقاه البحّارة في البحر.

safrica.seen: Tswana: Gakgala, the mopane worm.

stories.title: The mopane worm
stories.text: The Tswana see the small diamond of Delphinus as Gakgala, the mopane worm, the caterpillar that is collected and eaten, which appears when these stars are prominent.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014)

af.seen: Tswana: Gakgala, die mopaniewurm.

stories.title: Die mopaniewurm
stories.text: Die Tswana sien die klein ruit van Delphinus as Gakgala, die mopaniewurm, die ruspe wat versamel en geëet word, en wat verskyn wanneer hierdie sterre hoog aan die hemel staan.

ar.seen: التسوانا: غاكغالا، دودة الموبان.

stories.title: دودة الموبان
stories.text: يرى التسوانا المعيّن الصغير في الدلفين «غاكغالا»، دودة الموبان، اليرقة التي تُجمع وتؤكل، وتظهر حين تعلو هذه النجوم.

arab.seen: Equuleus, "a piece of the horse": four tiny stars, "like a trace when the trace has worn away", fainter even than al-Suha, close to Sa'd al-Bahim in Pegasus. The poet says nothing came down from the Bedouins about any name for them.

full.e: It is followed by small stars, hidden, with no light;
in all they have been counted as four, scarcely showing out of the dark,
like a faded mark when the mark has worn away; the Greeks call them the Piece of the Horse.
Its stars are smaller than the star al-Suha; they lie near Sa'd al-Bahim.
Nothing has reached us about them from the Bedouins, no names and no titles.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 5 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: قطعة الفرس: أربعة كويكبات خفية «كأنها الرسم إذا الرسم اندرس»، أصغر من السُّها، قرب سعد البهام. ويقول الناظم إنه لم يأته عن الأعراب فيها شيء من الأسماء والألقاب.

greek.seen: The head of a little horse.

stories.title: The little horse
stories.text: This small constellation was added by Ptolemy, and there was never a strong myth for it. Some writers said it was Celeris, the brother or foal of Pegasus, given by Hermes to Castor. Others said it was the horse that Poseidon struck from the earth in his contest with Athena.
stories.source: Ptolemy, Almagest; later commentators

ar.seen: رأس حصان صغير.

stories.title: الحصان الصغير
stories.text: أضاف بطليموس هذه الكوكبة الصغيرة ولم تكن لها أسطورة قوية. قال بعض الكتّاب إنها سيليريس أخو بيغاسوس أو مهره، أهداه هرمس إلى كاستور، وقال آخرون إنها الحصان الذي ضرب بوسيدون الأرض فأخرجه في منافسته مع أثينا.

arab.seen: Pegasus, a great horse that the Greeks gave wings and only forelegs, with mane, rump and haunch, "larger than the Lion when the Lion rises". The Arabs named its stars as a series of Su'ud, "lucky stars": Sa'd al-Bahim, Sa'd al-Humam, Sa'd Bari', Sa'd Matar, along with al-Jahfala (the horse's lip). The four stars of the Great Square are al-Farghan, the two spouts, and are also called Nahiz al-Dalw, the bucket. Two stars between them are al-Karab, the knot that ties the bucket's rope.

stories.title: The great bucket of the sky
stories.text: Where the Greeks saw a winged horse, the Bedouin saw the most important object in desert life: a big leather well-bucket. The four stars of the Great Square are its mouth. Two stars are its Fargh (the spouts water pours from), and the cross-pieces that hold it open are its 'Arquwa. The rope, al-Rasha', hangs down through Andromeda to the star Batn al-Hut. When the bucket's stars set in autumn, the season of rain began. Ibn Qutayba quotes the old rhymed saying: "When the Bucket rises, the green fodder dries out, the young donkey sheds its coat, and the unmarried man looks for a wife", now that the hard winter is over.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); Commentary on the site (Abha al-Mawakib)

stories.title: Why so many 'lucky' stars?
stories.text: Ten star-pairs in this part of the sky are each called Sa'd, "good luck". There are the four that are lunar mansions (Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya) and six others, including Sa'd Nashira, Sa'd al-Malik, Sa'd al-Bahim, Sa'd al-Humam, Sa'd al-Bari' and Sa'd Matar. They rise at the end of winter, when the cold breaks, camels give birth and the grass returns, so the Arabs felt their rising brought good fortune.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: After them comes a figure called the Horse, stars mostly like burning brands;
the sages of the Greeks have likened it to a horse of mighty appearance,
with a wing and two forelegs; its hind legs are missing from its shape;

a: يربو من الليث إذا الليث استقل
full.e: with mane-root, croup and haunch, larger than the Lion when the Lion rises.
On its head you see two stars, two hand-spans apart;
the Arabs call them Sa'd al-Bahim; when they shine they are followed by a star
which they also call al-Jahfala, the horse's lip, shining in the sky for whoever looks at it;
and after it two dim stars, close to the Sa'd,
lying on the horse's mane: one who surely knows has told
that among the Bedouins of Yemen they have been named Sa'd al-Humam, know it.
After them rise two stars on the horse's chest, both dim,
near a bright, gleaming star: the Arabs named them Sa'd Bari'.
After them rises Sa'd Matar, a star so small it escapes the eye,

a: هما على الركبة من هذا الفرس
full.e: and a star near it like a firebrand; both lie on the knee of this horse.
In the figure of the steed are four stars which you see as a broad square;
among the Arabs they are known as the two Spouts, and 'the Bucket' is also their name.
In the middle of the two Spouts are two stars, both on the horse's flank;

a: خبّر بعضُ من روى من العرب
full.e: some who report from the Arabs say they are called the Knot of the bucket-rope.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 18 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الفرس الأعظم: فرس عظيم جعل له الإغريق جناحًا ويدين بلا رجلين. وسمّى العرب نجومه سلسلة من السعود: سعد البهام وسعد الهُمام وسعد البارع وسعد مطر، ومعها الجحفلة. والنجوم الأربعة في المربّع هي الفَرغان وتسمّى ناهز الدلو، ونجمان بينهما هما الكَرَب أي عقدة حبل الدلو.

stories.title: الدلو العظيم في السماء
stories.text: حيث رأى الإغريق فرسًا مجنحًا رأى أهل البادية أهمّ شيء في حياتهم: دلوًا كبيرًا من الجلد. فالمربّع الكبير فمه، والفرغان مصبّاه اللذان يسيل منهما الماء، والعَرقُوتان خشبتاه المعترضتان، والرِّشاء حبله يتدلّى عبر المرأة المسلسلة إلى بطن الحوت. وكان سقوط نجوم الدلو في الخريف إيذانًا بموسم المطر. وينقل ابن قتيبة سجع العرب: «إذا طلع الدلو، هِيبَ الجزو، وأنسل العفو، وطلب اللهوَ الخِلْو»، أي جفّ الرطب من الكلأ، ونسل ولد الحمار وبره، وطلب العَزَب الزواج بعد شدّة الشتاء.

stories.title: لماذا كثرت السعود؟
stories.text: في هذه الناحية عشرة أزواج من النجوم كل منها «سعد»: أربعة من المنازل (سعد الذابح وسعد بلع وسعد السعود وسعد الأخبية)، وستة غيرها منها سعد ناشرة وسعد الملك وسعد البهام وسعد الهمام وسعد البارع وسعد مطر. وهي تطلع في آخر الشتاء حين ينكسر البرد وتُنتج الإبل ويعود العشب، فتيمّن العرب بطلوعها.

greek.seen: Pegasus, the winged horse.

stories.title: Pegasus and Bellerophon
stories.text: Pegasus sprang from the blood of Medusa when Perseus cut off her head. The hero Bellerophon tamed him with a golden bridle from Athena and rode him to kill the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster. Proud of his victories, Bellerophon tried to fly up to Olympus, the home of the gods. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting Pegasus, and Bellerophon fell back to earth, while Pegasus flew on into the sky. Only the front half of the horse appears in the stars.
stories.source: Kitab al-Sama'; Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: بيغاسوس الحصان المجنّح.

stories.title: بيغاسوس وبيليروفون
stories.text: خرج بيغاسوس من دم ميدوسا حين قطع برسيوس رأسها. فروّضه البطل بيليروفون بلجام ذهبي من أثينا، وركبه ليقتل الكيميرا الوحش النافث للنار. فلمّا اغترّ بانتصاراته حاول أن يطير إلى الأولمب مسكن الآلهة، فأرسل زيوس ذبابة لسعت بيغاسوس فسقط بيليروفون إلى الأرض، وواصل بيغاسوس طيرانه إلى السماء. ولا يظهر في النجوم إلا النصف الأمامي من الحصان.

arab.seen: Andromeda, "the Chained Woman", joined to the Horse. Its bright star at the waist is al-Rasha', "the bucket rope", also called Batn al-Hut, "the belly of the fish", the last of the 28 lunar mansions. A star below the leg is al-'Anaq ("'Anaq al-Ard", the caracal, a desert lynx). Three stars and a fourth on her hand are Ra's al-Naqa, the head of the great she-camel whose body is Cassiopeia. The poet notes that the name Andromeda is also famous.

stories.title: The rope of the bucket
stories.text: The bright star at Andromeda's waist was the end of the long rope of the great sky-bucket (see Pegasus). That's why it is called al-Rasha'. As the last lunar mansion, it was also the belly of a great fish lying across Andromeda and Pisces, Batn al-Hut. The modern name Mirach comes from Arabic mi'zar, "waist-cloth".
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); Commentary on the site (Abha al-Mawakib)

full.e: It is followed by the stars of the Chained Woman, stars all joined
to the second Horse; among them is a star of light that is called the Rope,
one of the bright and shining stars, and in the woman it marks the waist;
it is, you should know, the last of the lunar mansions, as the ancients told us,
and it is the one called the Belly of the Fish: certain knowledge, not guesswork.
And a star of hers just below the leg the Bedouins know as al-'Anaq,
and it may be called 'Anaq al-Ard, the caracal; so some report from others.

a: ثم على الراحة منها قد تجد
full.e: Then on her palm you will find three stars, and one alone apart,
bright and glittering in body: these are called the Head of the She-Camel.
And Andromeda is a name of this figure, by which it has become famous.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 10 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: المرأة المسلسلة متصلة بنجوم الفرس. نجمها النيّر على الخصر هو الرِّشاء، أي حبل الدلو، ويسمّى بطن الحوت وهو آخر منازل القمر. ونجم تحت الساق هو العَناق (عناق الأرض، الوشق). وثلاثة كواكب ورابع منفرد على راحتها هي رأس الناقة التي جسدها ذات الكرسي. ويذكر الناظم أن اسم أندروميدا مشهور أيضًا.

stories.title: حبل الدلو
stories.text: النجم النيّر على خصر المرأة المسلسلة هو طرف الحبل الطويل لدلو السماء العظيم (انظر الفرس الأعظم)، ولذلك سُمّي «الرشاء». ولأنه آخر منازل القمر كان أيضًا بطن حوت عظيم ممتدّ عبر المرأة المسلسلة والحوت، «بطن الحوت». واسم Mirach الحديث من «المِئزر».

greek.seen: Princess Andromeda, chained to a rock.

stories.title: The chained princess
stories.text: Because of her mother Cassiopeia's boast, Andromeda was chained to a rock by the sea as a sacrifice to the monster Cetus. Perseus, flying home with Medusa's head, saw her, fell in love, and killed the monster. They married, and Athena placed Andromeda in the sky near her husband and her parents, her arms still stretched out as if in chains.
stories.source: Kitab al-Sama'; Ovid, Metamorphoses 4

ar.seen: الأميرة أندروميدا مقيّدة إلى صخرة.

stories.title: الأميرة المسلسلة
stories.text: بسبب تباهي أمها كاسيوبيا قُيّدت أندروميدا إلى صخرة على البحر قربانًا للوحش قيطس. فرآها برسيوس عائدًا طائرًا برأس ميدوسا فأحبّها وقتل الوحش. فتزوّجا، ووضعت أثينا أندروميدا في السماء قرب زوجها وأبويها، وذراعاها ما زالتا ممدودتين كأنهما في السلاسل.

arab.seen: Triangulum: four stars, two bright and two faint, rising opposite the Ram. The poet gives the two brighter stars the name al-Anisan and admits he doesn't know the names of the smaller pair. With this, the northern constellations are finished.

full.e: After it, turn back to the Triangle: when al-'Anaq rises it does not delay;
look for its rising opposite the star of the Ram; its stars, when counted, are four;
two of its stars are bright, and the other two are faint;
al-Anisan is the name of the two brighter, and I do not know the name of the smaller two.
Now the stars of the north have passed, described in the briefest words.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 5 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: المثلث: أربعة كواكب، اثنان نيّران واثنان خفيّان، تطلع حيال نجم الكبش. يسمّي الناظم النيّرين الأنيسان ويعترف أنه لا يدري اسم الأصغرين. وبه تنتهي الكوكبات الشمالية.

greek.seen: A triangle: the Nile delta, or the island of Sicily.

stories.title: A shape from the land
stories.text: The Greeks called it Deltoton, after the shape of the Greek letter delta. Some said Hermes placed it in the sky to show the outline of the Nile delta. Others said it was the triangular island of Sicily, placed there at the request of Demeter, the goddess of grain, who loved the island.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia; Hyginus

ar.seen: مثلّث: دلتا النيل أو جزيرة صقلية.

stories.title: شكل من الأرض
stories.text: سمّاه الإغريق «دلتوتون» على شكل الحرف اليوناني دلتا. فقال بعضهم إن هرمس وضعه في السماء ليُري شكل دلتا النيل، وقال آخرون إنه جزيرة صقلية المثلّثة، وُضعت هناك بطلب من ديميتر إلهة الحبوب التي كانت تحبّ الجزيرة.

arab.seen: The first of the zodiac, the Ram. A large star sits on its nose, where the Greek astronomer Hipparchus ("Burkhis") placed it. Two stars are al-Sharatan, "the two signs", and the brighter is al-Natih, "the butter" (Hamal). With a third star they are al-Ashrat. Three faint stars on the Ram's belly are al-Butayn, "the little belly", and look as if they are hiding out of shyness. Small stars above them are Rijl al-Ghul, the ghoul's foot.

stories.title: The two signs of spring
stories.text: Al-Sharatan were the first of the lunar mansions and the sign that spring had begun. Ibn Qutayba gives the Bedouin rhymed saying for their rising: "When al-Sharatan rise, time becomes even, people come home, and neighbours exchange gifts." The desert pools had dried up, so the tribes left the open steppe and came back to their own wells. Families who had spent the season apart met again and gave each other presents. Ibn Qutayba also records a belief that God created the world with the Sun at the head of the Ram, when day and night were equal.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: Now let us mention, step by step, the stars of the figures of the zodiac.

a: يبدو من الأفق إذا الغفر أفل
full.e: The first is the Ram, which is called al-Hamal; it rises from the horizon as al-Ghafr sets;
as if the seller were following its track; its stars are thirteen.
Among them is a star of great body, which Hipparchus places as the muzzle.
It is followed by a star of the Ram whose light is less than the light of the first;
the Arabs named them the Two Signs, and the brighter of the two is sometimes called
the Butter; and some add a star that shines upon its horns
to the Two Signs, and so call them the Butting and the Signs as well, know this.
And sometimes the two brightest of them are called, know it, the Two Signs: report it so.
After them follow the stars of al-Butayn, three, that charm the beauty of the eye,
faint, upon the belly of the Ram, as though they were hiding out of shyness.
Above them are small stars, left outside this figure;
they are called the Ghoul's Foot among the Arabs, and they lie near Perseus.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 13 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الحمل، أول البروج. نجم عظيم على خطمه جعله برخيس (هيبرخس) هناك. ونجمان هما الشَّرَطان، وأنورهما الناطح، ومع نجم ثالث تسمّى الأشراط. وثلاثة نجوم خفية على بطن الحمل هي البُطَين «كأنهن مستترات من خجل». ونجوم صغار فوقها هي رِجل الغول.

stories.title: علامتا الربيع
stories.text: الشرطان أول منازل القمر وعلامة أول الربيع. يذكر ابن قتيبة سجع العرب في طلوعهما: «إذا طلع الشرطان، استوى الزمان، وحضرت الأوطان، وتهادى الجيران». أي قلّت الغدران في البادية فرجع الناس إلى مياههم وأوطانهم، والتقى من كانوا متفرّقين في النُّجعة فأهدى بعضهم إلى بعض. ويروي ابن قتيبة أيضًا أنه يقال إن الله خلق الخلق والشمس برأس الحمل والليل والنهار متساويان.

greek.seen: The ram with the golden fleece.

stories.title: The golden ram
stories.text: The children Phrixus and Helle were in danger from their cruel stepmother, so their mother sent a flying ram with a golden fleece to rescue them. As it flew over the sea, Helle slipped off and drowned in the strait that was named the Hellespont after her. Phrixus reached Colchis safely, sacrificed the ram to Zeus, and hung up its golden fleece. That is the same Golden Fleece that Jason and the Argonauts later sailed to find. Zeus placed the ram in the sky.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: الكبش ذو الصوف الذهبي.

stories.title: الكبش الذهبي
stories.text: كان الطفلان فريكسوس وهيلي في خطر من زوجة أبيهما القاسية، فأرسلت أمهما كبشًا طائرًا صوفه من ذهب لينقذهما. وبينما كان يطير فوق البحر انزلقت هيلي فغرقت في المضيق الذي سُمّي باسمها «الهلسبونت». ووصل فريكسوس سالمًا إلى كولخيس فذبح الكبش قربانًا لزيوس وعلّق صوفه الذهبي، وهو الجزّة الذهبية التي أبحر جاسون والأرغونوت فيما بعد للبحث عنها. فرفع زيوس الكبش إلى السماء.

arab.seen: Taurus. Stars on its hump, which the Greeks make its back and "about which the Arabs say a great deal", are al-Thurayya, the Pleiades, also simply called al-Najm, "the Star", and a lunar mansion. After them comes a great, beautiful red star with many names: al-Dabaran ("the follower"), al-Mijdah, al-Fanīq (the prize stallion camel), Tabi' al-Najm, Tali al-Najm, and al-Hadi, the camel-driver. It was thought unlucky. Two close stars are al-Diqa, "the narrow gap", or al-Kalban, the two dogs, and the stars around are al-Qilas, the young she-camels.

stories.title: Al-Dabaran's proposal
stories.text: Al-Dabaran fell in love with al-Thurayya and wanted to marry her. He sent the Moon to ask for her hand. But al-Thurayya turned him down and walked away. She asked the Moon, "What would I do with this penniless pauper (al-subrut), who owns nothing?" So al-Dabaran gathered his little herd of young she-camels, al-Qilas (the Hyades cluster), to show he had property. Ever since, he follows her wherever she goes across the sky, driving his camels in front of him as her bride-price, with his two dogs at his heels. He never catches up. His name comes from this: al-Dabaran, "the one who comes behind". The poet Dhu al-Rumma wrote: "Her Dabaran creeps along upon her tracks: he is never left behind, and never catches up."
stories.source: Arab tradition recorded in the anwa' books; Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.) (for al-Qilas and the two dogs); Kitab al-Sama'

stories.title: The unlucky star
stories.text: Because it always follows the much-loved Pleiades, al-Dabaran got the blame. The Arabs called his rain-season unlucky and thought a year whose rain came under al-Dabaran would be a year of drought. Proverbs were made from the story: "more ill-omened than the camel-driver of the Star", and, for the girl who refused him, "more faithless than al-Thurayya".
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); al-Marzuqi, al-Azmina wa al-Amkina (11th c.)

full.e: After it comes the Bull, and among its stars are stars shining above its withers;
the Greeks make them its hump, and the Arabs have a great deal to say about them.
They are called al-Thurayya, and sometimes all of them are called simply 'the Star';
they are also one of the mansions of the Moon, known to the desert people and the townsfolk.
After it comes a great, glowing star, adorned with light and a red colour,
lovely to look at, elegant in appearance, known as al-Mijdah and al-Fanīq;
'Follower of the Star' is another of its names, and al-Dabaran is its name among the Arabs.
They may also call it the One Behind the Star, as we have heard, and they may call
this star al-Mijdah and the Camel-Driver; and every poet has mentioned it in his verse.
With them it is an ill-omened star, and its rain-season is disliked and blamed.
It is followed by two brilliant stars, a hand-span apart, which are called
the Narrow Gap by the Bedouins; and around it you see stars blazing,
known to the Bedouins as the Young She-Camels (of this, know, I have no doubt);
and the Arabs call the two stars that almost touch the Two Dogs.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 14 couplets for this constellation

quran.en: By the Star when it falls.
quran.note: Many early commentators, among them Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, said 'the Star' here is al-Thurayya, the Pleiades, setting at dawn (Ibn Kathir). The Arabs often called the Pleiades simply 'al-Najm', the Star.
quran.noteAr: قال مجاهد وغيره إن النجم هنا هو الثريا إذا سقطت مع الفجر، والعرب تسمّي الثريا النجم.

ar.seen: الثور. كواكب على سنامه «والعرب فيها تكثر الكلاما» هي الثريا وتسمّى النجم وهي من منازل القمر. ويتبعها نجم عظيم أحمر جميل كثير الأسماء: الدَّبَران والمِجدح والفنيق وتابع النجم وتالي النجم والحادي، وكانت العرب تتشاءم به. ونجمان متقاربان هما الضِّيقة أو الكلبان، والنجوم حولها القِلاص.

stories.title: خطبة الدبران
stories.text: أحبّ الدبرانُ الثريا وأراد أن يتزوّجها، فأرسل القمر يخطبها له. فأبت عليه وولّت عنه، وقالت للقمر: «ما أصنع بهذا السُّبروت الذي لا مال له؟». فجمع الدبران قلاصه (عنقود القلائص) يتموّل بها، فهو يتبعها حيثما توجّهت في السماء يسوق صداقها أمامه وكلباه خلفه، ولا يلحقها أبدًا. ومن هنا اسمه «الدبران» لأنه يأتي في دبرها. قال ذو الرمة: «يدبّ على آثارها دبرانُها ... فلا هو مسبوقٌ ولا هو يلحقُ».

stories.title: النجم المشؤوم
stories.text: لأنه يتبع الثريا المحبوبة دائمًا نال الدبران اللوم، فذمّت العرب نوءه وزعمت أن السنة التي تُمطر بنوئه تكون مجدبة. وجرت من الحكاية أمثال: «أشأم من حادي النجم»، وفي الفتاة التي ردّته: «أغدر من الثريا».

greek.seen: The white bull who carried off Europa; on its back, the Pleiades and Hyades.

stories.title: Europa and the bull
stories.text: Zeus fell in love with the princess Europa, who was gathering flowers with her friends by the sea. He turned himself into a beautiful white bull and lay down among the flowers. When Europa climbed onto his back, he plunged into the sea and swam with her to Crete, where she bore him three sons, among them Minos. The continent of Europe is named after her.
stories.source: Kitab al-Sama'; Ovid, Metamorphoses 2

stories.title: The seven sisters and their weeping sisters
stories.text: The Pleiades were the seven daughters of Atlas. The giant hunter Orion chased them for years until Zeus turned them into doves, and then into stars. One of the seven is faint, and it was said she hides in shame, or in grief. Close by are the Hyades, the sisters who nursed the baby Dionysus. When their brother Hyas was killed, they wept so much that they became stars, and their tears were thought to bring the rains of spring and autumn.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia; Kitab al-Sama'

poem.orig:
Δέδυκε μὲν ἀ σελάννα
καὶ Πληΐαδες· μέσαι δὲ
νύκτες, πάρα δ᾽ ἔρχετ᾽ ὤρα,
ἐγὼ δὲ μόνα κατεύδω.
poem.trans:
The moon has set,
and the Pleiades; it is the middle
of the night, the hour goes by,
and I sleep alone.
poem.by: Attributed to Sappho (7th–6th century BCE)

ar.seen: الثور الأبيض الذي اختطف أوروبا، وعلى ظهره الثريا والقلائص.

stories.title: أوروبا والثور
stories.text: أحبّ زيوس الأميرة أوروبا وهي تجمع الزهور مع صاحباتها قرب البحر، فتحوّل إلى ثور أبيض جميل واستلقى بين الزهور. فلمّا ركبت أوروبا ظهره اندفع إلى البحر وسبح بها إلى كريت، حيث ولدت له ثلاثة أبناء منهم مينوس. وقارة أوروبا مسمّاة باسمها.

stories.title: الأخوات السبع وأخواتهن الباكيات
stories.text: الثريا بنات أطلس السبع. ظلّ الصيّاد العملاق أوريون يطاردهن سنين حتى حوّلهن زيوس حمامات ثم نجومًا. وإحدى السبع خافتة، فقيل إنها تختبئ خجلًا أو حزنًا. وبقربهن القلائص (الهياديس)، الأخوات اللواتي أرضعن ديونيسوس الطفل؛ فلمّا قُتل أخوهن هياس بكين حتى صرن نجومًا، وكان يُظنّ أن دموعهن تأتي بأمطار الربيع والخريف.

stories.title: The cluster gathered together
stories.text: The Japanese name for the Pleiades, Subaru, means 'to gather into one' or 'to unite'. Around a thousand years ago the court lady Sei Shōnagon named it the finest of all stars. The car company Subaru took its name and its six-star badge from the cluster.
stories.source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book; Wikipedia, 'Pleiades'

poem.orig:
星はすばる。ひこぼし。ゆふづつ。
よばひ星、すこしをかし。
poem.trans:
Of stars: Subaru (the Pleiades). Hikoboshi (Altair). The evening star.
Shooting stars are a little charming too.
poem.by: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book, section 'Stars' (around 1000)

ar.seen: سوبارو، الثريا، «المجتمعة».

stories.title: العنقود المجتمع
stories.text: الاسم الياباني للثريا «سوبارو» معناه «الجمع في واحد» أو «الاتحاد». وقبل نحو ألف سنة جعلتها سيدة البلاط سي شوناغون أجمل النجوم كلها. وأخذت شركة السيارات سوبارو اسمها وشعارها ذا النجوم الست من هذا العنقود.

stories.title: The six mothers of Kartikeya
stories.text: The Pleiades are the Krittikas, six mothers who nursed the war god Kartikeya (Skanda), born from the fire of Shiva. He grew six heads so he could feed from all six at once, and was named after them.
stories.source: Mahabharata; Skanda Purana

stories.title: Rohini, the Moon's favourite wife
stories.text: The 27 lunar mansions (nakshatras) are the 27 daughters of Daksha, all married to the Moon god Chandra. But the Moon loved only Rohini (Aldebaran). The other wives complained to their father, and Daksha cursed the Moon to waste away. The gods softened the curse so that he wastes away and grows again each month, which is why the Moon waxes and wanes.
stories.source: Puranas; Mahabharata

ar.seen: كريتيكا (الثريا) وروهيني (الدبران).

stories.title: أمهات كارتيكيا الست
stories.text: الثريا هي «الكريتيكا»، ست أمهات أرضعن إله الحرب كارتيكيا (سكاندا) المولود من نار شيفا، فنبتت له ستة رؤوس ليرضع منهن جميعًا معًا، وسُمّي باسمهن.

stories.title: روهيني، زوجة القمر المفضّلة
stories.text: منازل القمر السبع والعشرون هي بنات داكشا السبع والعشرون، تزوّجهن جميعًا إله القمر تشاندرا، لكنه لم يحبّ إلا روهيني (الدبران). فشكت الأخريات إلى أبيهن، فلعن داكشا القمر بأن يذوي. وخفّف الآلهة اللعنة فصار يذوي ثم ينمو كل شهر، ولذلك يتزايد القمر ويتناقص.

safrica.seen: Khoikhoi: the Pleiades are wives, Aldebaran their husband. Sotho: Selemela. Zulu and Xhosa: isiLimela.

stories.title: The husband who missed (Khoikhoi)
stories.text: The Pleiades, Khunuseti ('stars of spring'), are the daughters of the sky god Tsui-||Goab. They sent their husband Aldebaran out to hunt three zebras (Orion's belt), and told him not to come home without meat. He had only one arrow. He shot it and missed, and the arrow (Orion's sword) fell short beyond the zebras. A fierce lion (Betelgeuse) sits watching the zebras, so Aldebaran cannot go and fetch his arrow. He is afraid to go home empty-handed, so he sits out in the cold night sky, shivering and hungry.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014); Royal Museums Greenwich, 'South African star myths'

stories.title: The digging stars
stories.text: For the Sotho and Tswana the Pleiades are Selemela, and for the Zulu and Xhosa isiLimela, 'the digging stars'. When they appear before dawn in winter, it is time to begin hoeing the fields. Xhosa men counted their years of manhood from the June rising of isiLimela, which marked the end of initiation school. Sotho travellers navigated by them: keep the Southern Cross on your left and the Pleiades on your right to travel west.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014); Royal Museums Greenwich, 'South African star myths'

stories.title: The hartebeest (/Xam San)
stories.text: The /Xam San saw Aldebaran as a male hartebeest, with Betelgeuse as his mate. They called the Pleiades 'the things of summer'.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014)

af.seen: Khoikhoi: die Sewe Susters is vroue, en Aldebaran is hulle man. Sotho: Selemela. Zoeloe en Xhosa: isiLimela.

stories.title: Die man wat mis geskiet het (Khoikhoi)
stories.text: Die Sewe Susters, Khunuseti ('sterre van die lente'), is die dogters van die hemelgod Tsui-||Goab. Hulle het hul man Aldebaran gestuur om drie sebras (Orion se gordel) te gaan jag, en gesê hy moet nie sonder vleis terugkom nie. Hy het net een pyl gehad. Hy het geskiet en mis, en die pyl (Orion se swaard) het kort van die sebras neergeval. 'n Kwaai leeu (Betelgeuse) sit en die sebras dophou, en daarom kan Aldebaran nie sy pyl gaan haal nie. Hy is bang om met leë hande huis toe te gaan, en daarom sit hy daar buite in die koue naghemel, bewend en honger.

stories.title: Die grawe-sterre
stories.text: Vir die Sotho en Tswana is die Sewe Susters Selemela, en vir die Zoeloe en Xhosa isiLimela, 'die grawe-sterre'. Wanneer hulle in die winter voor dagbreek verskyn, is dit tyd om die lande te begin skoffel. Xhosa-mans het hul jare van manlikheid getel vanaf die Junie-opkoms van isiLimela, wat die einde van die inisiasieskool aangedui het. Sotho-reisigers het met hulle die pad gevind: hou die Suiderkruis aan jou linkerhand en die Sewe Susters aan jou regterhand om wes te reis.

stories.title: Die hartbees (/Xam San)
stories.text: Die /Xam San het Aldebaran gesien as 'n hartbeesbul, met Betelgeuse as sy maat. Hulle het die Sewe Susters 'die dinge van die somer' genoem.

ar.seen: الخويخوي: الثريا زوجات والدبران زوجهن. السوتو: سيليميلا. الزولو والخوسا: إيسيليميلا.

stories.title: الزوج الذي أخطأ الرمية (الخويخوي)
stories.text: الثريا «خونوسيتي» أي «نجوم الربيع» بنات إله السماء تسوي-غواب. أرسلن زوجهن الدبران ليصطاد ثلاثة حُمُر وحش (حزام الجبّار) وقلن له ألّا يعود بلا لحم. ولم يكن معه إلا سهم واحد، فرمى فأخطأ، وسقط السهم (سيف الجبّار) دون الحُمُر. وأسد ضارٍ (منكب الجوزاء) يجلس يراقب الحُمُر، فلا يستطيع الدبران أن يذهب ليأتي بسهمه، ويخاف أن يعود إلى البيت خالي اليدين، فيبقى جالسًا في ليل السماء البارد يرتجف جائعًا.

stories.title: نجوم الحفر
stories.text: الثريا عند السوتو والتسوانا «سيليميلا»، وعند الزولو والخوسا «إيسيليميلا» أي «نجوم الحفر». فإذا ظهرت قبل الفجر في الشتاء حان وقت عزق الحقول. وكان رجال الخوسا يعدّون سنوات رجولتهم من طلوع إيسيليميلا في يونيو الذي يؤذن بنهاية مدرسة التنشئة. واهتدى مسافرو السوتو بها: اجعل الصليب الجنوبي عن يسارك والثريا عن يمينك لتسير غربًا.

stories.title: ظبي الهارتبيست (/زام السان)
stories.text: رأى /زام السان الدبران ذكرَ ظبي «هارتبيست»، ومنكب الجوزاء أنثاه، وسمّوا الثريا «أشياء الصيف».

arab.seen: Gemini, which the poet calls by its old Arabic name al-Jawza'. The Greeks saw two twins. The two stars on their heads (Castor and Pollux) are al-Dhira', the forearm. Other stars are al-Han'a, al-Zirr and al-Maysan, the feet of one twin. Three faint stars curved like a bending archer are Qaws al-Jabbar, the Giant's bow (al-Jawza''s bow), from which he shoots "with the forearm of the figure". Small stars around are al-Azfar, the claws.

stories.title: The paw of the Arab Lion
stories.text: The Arabs' Lion (al-Asad) was enormous, much bigger than the Greek Leo. It stretched from Gemini all the way to Virgo. Its two front paws (forearms) were Castor and Pollux, al-Dhira' al-Maqbuda, "the drawn-in forearm", and the pair Procyon and Gomeisa, al-Dhira' al-Mabsuta, "the outstretched forearm". Ibn Qutayba gives the rhymed saying for when the forearm rises in high summer: "When the Forearm rises, the Sun throws off her veil, the horizon blazes with rays, and the mirage shimmers over every plain."
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: It is followed by the stars of al-Jawza', stars that shine out in the darkness;
the Greeks likened them to Twins; on their two heads you see two stars,
both known as the Forearm; and the brighter, the shining one with rays,
is called the foremost of the two Forearms; between them, know it, to the eye,
are five hand-spans; and if we search opposite it, we find al-Han'a:
two stars of this figure, followed by bright stars;
two of them are called al-Zirr, the Button, and al-Han'a, and al-Maysan;
they are the feet of one of the Twins, two hand-spans apart when you measure them.
And the stars of the two feet are among stars bright and blooming in the darkness;
in their rising they go before stars of which you see only dim ones,
three, with the feet, curved like an archer's bend;
the Bedouins named it the Bow of the Giant, and some reporters of stories say
it is his bow with its string drawn, from which he shoots with the figure's forearm.
Around the Forearm are small stars which they named the Claws.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 14 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: التوأمان، ويسمّيهما الناظم باسمهما العربي القديم الجوزاء. على رأسيهما نجمان هما الذراع، وفيها الهَنعة والزِّرّ والميسان وهي قدما أحد التوأمين. وثلاثة كواكب خافتة منحنية «كانحناء الرامي» هي قوس الجبّار، يرمي عنها «بذراع الصورة». وكواكب صغار حولها هي الأظفار.

stories.title: ذراع الأسد العربي
stories.text: كان أسد العرب عظيمًا يمتد من التوأمين إلى العذراء، وذراعاه نجمان نجمان: الذراع المقبوضة (رأسا التوأمين)، والذراع المبسوطة (الشعرى الغميصاء ومرزمها). وينقل ابن قتيبة سجع العرب في طلوع الذراع في شدة الصيف: «إذا طلعت الذراع، حسرت الشمسُ القناع، وأشعلت في الأفق الشعاع، وترقرق السرابُ بكلّ قاع».

greek.seen: The twins Castor and Pollux.

stories.title: The brothers who shared immortality
stories.text: Castor and Pollux were twin brothers, sons of Leda. Pollux was the son of Zeus and immortal, and Castor was the son of a mortal king. They sailed with the Argonauts and became the protectors of sailors. When Castor was killed in battle, Pollux begged Zeus to let him share his immortality with his brother. Zeus agreed, and the two spend alternate days on Olympus and in the underworld, side by side among the stars.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia; Ovid, Fasti 5

ar.seen: التوأمان كاستور وبولوكس.

stories.title: الأخوان اللذان تقاسما الخلود
stories.text: كاستور وبولوكس أخوان توأمان ابنا ليدا: بولوكس ابن زيوس خالد، وكاستور ابن ملك فانٍ. أبحرا مع الأرغونوت وصارا حاميين للبحّارة. فلمّا قُتل كاستور في معركة توسّل بولوكس إلى زيوس أن يقاسم أخاه خلوده، فقبل زيوس، فهما يقضيان يومًا في الأولمب ويومًا في العالم السفلي، متجاورين بين النجوم.

safrica.seen: /Xam San: Castor and Pollux are the eland's wives.

stories.title: The eland's wives
stories.text: Castor and Pollux are the two wives of the eland Procyon (see Canis Minor), according to the /Xam San.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014)

af.seen: /Xam San: Castor en Pollux is die eland se vroue.

stories.title: Die eland se vroue
stories.text: Castor en Pollux is die twee vroue van die eland Procyon (sien Canis Minor), volgens die /Xam San.

ar.seen: /زام السان: رأسا التوأمين زوجتا الإلند.

stories.title: زوجتا الإلند
stories.text: رأسا التوأمين عند /زام السان زوجتا ظبي الإلند الذي هو الشعرى الشامية (انظر الكلب الأصغر).

arab.seen: Cancer: nine faint stars gathered around a nebula (the Beehive cluster). Greek-trained astronomers called the nebula al-Ma'laf, the manger. The Arabs called it al-Lahat (the Lion's uvula) and al-Nathra, the Lion's nostril. Two faint stars after it are "the two donkeys" (a translated name; the Arabs called them the Lion's nostrils). Then comes al-Tarf, the Lion's eye, and small stars between are al-Ashfar, the eyelashes.

stories.title: The Lion's face
stories.text: In the Arab sky the whole of Cancer is the face of the great Lion. The misty Beehive cluster is his nostril, al-Nathra (the word also means the spray of a sneeze). The stars beside it are his nose, al-Tarf is his glaring eye, and the tiny stars are his eyelashes. Its rhymed saying from Ibn Qutayba: "When al-Nathra rises, the dates turn dark red, the palms are harvested at dawn, the herds stay close to the tents, and not a drop is left in any udder." This was the season for weaning the young.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); Commentary on the site (Abha al-Mawakib)

full.e: The Crab follows al-Jawza': stars that have lost their light;
when you count them they are nine, all gathered in one patch,
around a nebula called the Manger, and known, you should know, as the Uvula;
it is the one that all the Bedouins and the experts know as al-Nathra.
It is followed by two dim stars, which are called the Two Donkeys.
And al-Tarf is two stars, when they are counted, both of them very faint:

a: نجمٌ على المنخر من شكل الأسد
full.e: one star on the nostril of the Lion's figure, and another that the observers count
among the stars that belong to no figure, yet are observed and recorded;
between them are small stars that the Bedouins know as the Eyelashes.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 9 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: السرطان: تسعة كواكب خفية حول سحابي سمّاه علماء الفلك المِعلف، وسمّاه العرب اللَّهاة والنثرة، أي أنف الأسد. ويتبعه نجمان خفيّان سُمّيا الحمارين (وهو اسم مترجم، والعرب تسمّيهما منخري الأسد)، ثم الطَّرف أي عين الأسد، وكواكب صغار بينهما هي الأشفار.

stories.title: وجه الأسد
stories.text: السرطان كله في سماء العرب وجه الأسد العظيم: لطخة النثرة أنفه (والنثرة أيضًا ما يتطاير من العطسة)، والنجمان بجانبها منخراه، والطرف عينه، والكواكب الدقيقة أشفاره. وسجعها عند ابن قتيبة: «إذا طلعت النثرة، قنأت البُسرة، وجُني النخل بُكرة، وأوت المواشي حُجرة، ولم تترك في ذات دَرٍّ قطرة»، وهو وقت فصال الأولاد.

greek.seen: The crab sent by Hera.

stories.title: The crab that bit Heracles
stories.text: While Heracles fought the many-headed Hydra in the swamps of Lerna, Hera, who hated him, sent a giant crab to pinch his feet and distract him. Heracles crushed it under his heel. Hera rewarded the little creature's loyalty by placing it in the sky. It is a faint constellation, as befits a small, unlucky hero.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: السرطان الذي أرسلته هيرا.

stories.title: السرطان الذي عضّ هرقل
stories.text: بينما كان هرقل يقاتل الهيدرا ذات الرؤوس الكثيرة في مستنقعات ليرنا، أرسلت هيرا التي تكرهه سرطانًا عظيمًا يقرص قدميه ليشغله، فسحقه هرقل بعقبه. فكافأت هيرا المخلوق الصغير على وفائه بأن وضعته في السماء. وهو كوكبة خافتة تليق ببطل صغير سيّئ الحظ.

arab.seen: Leo. Among its many bright stars is al-Maliki, "the royal star" (Regulus), which the Greeks made the Lion's heart. Before it is a row of stars "like burning pearls", al-Jabha, the Lion's forehead. Then come al-Zubra, two stars on the Lion's back also called al-Kharatan, and Qunb al-Asad. A bright guiding star is al-Sarfa, "the Turning" (Denebola), by which travellers find their way. A dim cluster above is al-Hulba or al-Dafira, the tuft of the Lion's tail.

stories.title: The great Lion of the Arabs
stories.text: The Arab Lion covered a huge part of the sky. Its forearms are in Gemini and Canis Minor, its nose in Cancer, its eye (al-Tarf) and forehead (al-Jabha) in Leo, and its mane on its back (al-Zubra). Its tail-tuft (al-Hulba) reaches to Coma Berenices, and its two shins are the two Simaks, Arcturus and Spica. Seasons were marked by it. When its forehead rose at dawn in late summer, Suhail rose with it. The young camels were weaned, and the Arabs said: "When al-Jabha rises, the bereaved mothers moan for their young." They also said: "Without the rain of al-Jabha, the Arabs would have no camels."
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

stories.title: Al-Sarfa, the turning of the year
stories.text: The star at the Lion's tail is al-Sarfa, "the Turning". Ibn Qutayba explains: "It was called al-Sarfa because the heat turns away when it rises at dawn, and the cold turns away when it sets at dawn." The Arabs called it "the canine tooth of time", because it marks the bite between one season and the next.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: After the Crab comes the Lion: blooming stars, great in number,
among them a star called the Royal One, which you see among the brightest stars of the sky;
the Greeks make it the heart of the Lion; it follows stars that blaze like pearls,
set in a row as if they were a cloud: the Bedouins know them as the Forehead.
They are followed by al-Zubra, two stars, whose name with them is the Two Kharatan;
both are counted among the mansions, and among the Lion's stars, above the shoulders.
Around them are hidden stars, neither shining nor clear;
the Arabs know them as Qunb al-Asad; they are followed by a bright star by which
travellers find their way, called the Turning; above it are tangled stars,
dim, small in body, known as the Tail-Tuft and the Braid.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 10 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الأسد. فيه النجم الملكي الذي جعله الروم قلب الأسد، وأمامه نجوم «كاللآلئ تتقد» هي الجبهة، ثم الزُّبرة وهي نجمان على كاهل الأسد يسمّيان الخَراتان، وقُنب الأسد، ونجم نيّر يهتدي به السَّفر هو الصَّرفة، وكواكب ملتفّة فوقه هي الهُلبة أو الضفيرة.

stories.title: أسد العرب العظيم
stories.text: كان الأسد عند العرب يغطّي جزءًا عظيمًا من السماء: ذراعاه في التوأمين والكلب الأصغر، وأنفه في السرطان، وعينه (الطرف) وجبهته في الأسد، وزبرته على كاهله، وهلبته تمتد إلى الضفيرة، وساقاه السماكان. وكانت المواسم تُعرف به: إذا طلعت جبهته فجرًا في آخر الصيف طلع معها سهيل وفُصلت الفصلان، وقالت العرب: «إذا طلعت الجبهة، تحانّت الوَلَهة»، وقالت: «لولا نوء الجبهة ما كان للعرب إبل».

stories.title: الصرفة: انصراف الزمان
stories.text: النجم الذي عند ذنب الأسد هو «الصرفة». قال ابن قتيبة: «وسُمّي صرفةً لانصراف الحرّ عند طلوعها غُدوة، وانصراف البرد عند سقوطها غُدوة». وقالت العرب: «الصرفة ناب الدهر» لأنها تفترّ عن فصل الزمانين.

greek.seen: The Nemean lion.

stories.title: The lion with the impenetrable hide
stories.text: A lion with skin that no weapon could pierce was terrorising the land around Nemea. For his first labour Heracles tracked it to its cave, trapped it, and strangled it with his bare hands. He then skinned it using its own claws and wore the hide as a cloak and its head as a helmet. Zeus placed the lion in the sky.
stories.source: Kitab al-Sama'; Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: أسد نيميا.

stories.title: الأسد الذي لا يخترق جلده سلاح
stories.text: كان أسد لا يخترق جلده سلاح يروّع أرض نيميا. فتعقّبه هرقل في عمله الأول إلى كهفه، وحاصره وخنقه بيديه، ثم سلخه بمخالبه نفسها ولبس جلده عباءة ورأسه خوذة. ووضع زيوس الأسد في السماء.

egypt.seen: Mai, a lion between two crocodiles.

stories.title: The divine lion
stories.text: Egyptian star charts of the Ramesside period show a lion, Mai, called 'the divine lion between them', lying between two crocodiles. It is very likely our Leo, which the Mesopotamians and Greeks also saw as a lion. The lion was also linked to the Sun, because the Sun passed through these stars in high summer.
stories.source: Egyptian Streets, 'Ancient Egyptian constellations' (2024)

ar.seen: ماي، أسد بين تمساحين.

stories.title: الأسد الإلهي
stories.text: تُظهر خرائط النجوم المصرية من العصر الرعمسيسي أسدًا اسمه «ماي» يوصف بأنه «الأسد الإلهي بينهما» مستلقيًا بين تمساحين، وهو على الأرجح الأسد عندنا، الذي رآه أهل الرافدين والإغريق أسدًا أيضًا. وارتبط الأسد بالشمس لأنها تمرّ بهذه النجوم في عزّ الصيف.

safrica.seen: /Gwi San: Regulus is the 'fire-finisher'.

stories.title: The fire-finisher
stories.text: The /Gwi San call Regulus /edzini, 'the fire-finisher', because it sets only when the firewood has run out.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014)

af.seen: /Gwi San: Regulus is die 'vuur-klaarmaker'.

stories.title: Die vuur-klaarmaker
stories.text: Die /Gwi San noem Regulus /edzini, 'die vuur-klaarmaker', omdat hy eers ondergaan wanneer die brandhout op is.

ar.seen: سان /غوي: قلب الأسد «مُنهي النار».

stories.title: مُنهي النار
stories.text: يسمّي سان /غوي قلب الأسد «/إدزيني» أي مُنهي النار، لأنه لا يغيب إلا حين ينفد الحطب.

arab.seen: Virgo, also called al-Sunbula, the Ear of Wheat. Some of its stars, shaped like the letter lam, are al-'Awwa', "the Barker". After them comes a great clear star on the Maiden's hand, al-Simak al-A'zal (Spica), called "unarmed" because, unlike al-Simak al-Ramih, it has no lance. The Arabs made the two Simaks the shins of the Lion. Three small stars in a curve, "like the dots painted on a bride", are al-Ghafr, a lunar mansion.

stories.title: The dogs barking after the Lion
stories.text: The four stars of al-'Awwa' ("the Barker") stand behind the Lion. Ibn Qutayba says "they make them dogs following the Lion", a pack baying at the heels of the great beast. Their rising in autumn brought the first cold nights, and the Arabs said: "When al-'Awwa' rises, the tents are pitched, the air turns sweet, sleeping in the open is disliked, and the water-skins dry out."
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

stories.title: The best mansion of all
stories.text: The Arabs considered al-Ghafr the luckiest of the Moon's stations, especially for digging new wells. They said: "The best mansion for ever is between al-Zubana and the Lion", because the Lion's harmless tail lies on one side and the Scorpion's harmless claws on the other. Ibn Qutayba also records the belief that the prophets were born under al-Ghafr.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: It is followed by the Maiden, which is the Ear of Wheat: its stars are joined to its figure;
among them are stars that have filled with light, which the ancients named al-'Awwa', the Barker;
they are in the shape of the letter lam, shining to the eyes in the dark.
They are followed by a great, clear star, which they named al-Simak al-A'zal, the Unarmed;
it is on the hand of the Maiden, and rises after the rising of al-'Awwa';
the ancients made it a mansion of the Moon, and it is only called 'unarmed'
because it has no weapon, unlike the Lancer, which is given a lance to mark it;
and the Arabs made the two Simaks into the two shins of the fierce Lion.
It is followed by small stars that lie on the hem of this lady's robe,
three of them, set in a curve as if they were the painted dots on a bride;
all together they named them al-Ghafr, and made them a mansion of the Moon.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 11 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: العذراء، وتسمّى السنبلة. نجوم منها على شكل حرف اللام هي العوّاء. ويتبعها نجم عظيم على كفّ العذراء هو السماك الأعزل، سُمّي أعزل لأنه بلا سلاح بخلاف الرامح. وجعل العرب السماكين ساقي الأسد. وثلاثة كواكب صغار مقوّسة «كأنهن نُقَط العروس» هي الغَفر، منزل من منازل القمر.

stories.title: الكلاب تعوي خلف الأسد
stories.text: نجوم العوّاء الأربعة تقف خلف الأسد، قال ابن قتيبة: «وقد يجعلونها كلابًا تتبع الأسد»، كأنها كلاب تنبح عند عقب الوحش العظيم. وطلوعها في الخريف يأتي بأول الليالي الباردة، قال الساجع: «إذا طلعت العوّاء، ضُرب الخِباء، وطاب الهواء، وكُره العراء، وشُنّن السِّقاء».

stories.title: خير المنازل
stories.text: كانت العرب تعدّ الغفر أسعد منازل القمر، ولا سيما في استنباط المياه، وقالت: «خير منزلةٍ في الأبد، بين الزُّبانى والأسد»، لأنه يليه من الأسد ذنبه وليس يضرّ، ومن العقرب زباناها وليس تضرّ. ويروي ابن قتيبة أنهم قالوا: بالغفر يولد النبيّون.

greek.seen: A maiden holding an ear of wheat: Astraea, Demeter, or Persephone.

stories.title: The last goddess to leave the earth
stories.text: Virgo is often Astraea, the starry goddess of justice. In the Golden Age she lived among humans, but as people grew greedy and violent she withdrew, and she was the last of the immortals to leave the earth, rising into the sky as the Maiden. Next to her are the Scales of justice (Libra). Others saw her as Demeter, the grain goddess holding an ear of wheat (the star Spica), or as Erigone, daughter of Icarius (see Boötes).
stories.source: Aratus, Phaenomena 96–136; Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: عذراء تحمل سنبلة قمح: أستريا أو ديميتر أو برسيفوني.

stories.title: آخر إلهة غادرت الأرض
stories.text: كثيرًا ما تكون العذراء أستريا إلهة العدل النجمية. ففي العصر الذهبي عاشت بين البشر، فلمّا طغى عليهم الجشع والعنف انسحبت، وكانت آخر الخالدين مغادرةً للأرض، فصعدت إلى السماء عذراءَ، وبجانبها ميزان العدل. ورآها آخرون ديميتر إلهة الحبوب تحمل سنبلة (نجم السماك الأعزل)، أو إيريغوني ابنة إيكاريوس (انظر العوّاء).

stories.title: The bright jewel
stories.text: Spica is Chitra, 'the brilliant' or 'the beautiful', a lunar mansion ruled by Vishvakarma, the architect of the gods. A pearl or a bright lamp was its symbol. The month of Chaitra, in spring, takes its name from it.
stories.source: Wikipedia, 'Chitra (nakshatra)'

ar.seen: تشيترا، «المضيئة» (السماك الأعزل).

stories.title: الجوهرة المضيئة
stories.text: السماك الأعزل هو «تشيترا» أي البرّاقة الجميلة، منزل يحكمه فيشفاكارما مهندس الآلهة، ورمزه لؤلؤة أو سراج منير. ومنه أخذ شهر تشايترا في الربيع اسمه.

safrica.seen: Zulu: Spica is iNqonqoli, 'the wildebeest star'. //Gana San: 'the pig star'.

stories.title: The wildebeest star
stories.text: The Zulu call Spica iNqonqoli, 'the wildebeest star', because it is linked with the time when wildebeest give birth. The //Gana San called it 'the pig star'.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014)

af.seen: Zoeloe: Spica is iNqonqoli, 'die wildebees-ster'. //Gana San: 'die vark-ster'.

stories.title: Die wildebees-ster
stories.text: Die Zoeloe noem Spica iNqonqoli, 'die wildebees-ster', omdat dit verbind word met die tyd wanneer wildebeeste kalwers kry. Die //Gana San het dit 'die vark-ster' genoem.

ar.seen: الزولو: السماك الأعزل «إنكونكولي» نجم النو. سان //غانا: «نجم الخنزير».

stories.title: نجم النو
stories.text: يسمّي الزولو السماك الأعزل «إنكونكولي» أي نجم النو (الحيوان البرّي)، لأنه يرتبط بوقت ولادة النو. وسمّاه سان //غانا «نجم الخنزير».

arab.seen: Libra, the Balance. Its two bright stars, a lance's length apart, are al-Zubana. They are the two pans of the scale, and also the Scorpion's claws, and in summer they are "Zubana al-Sayf". Then the poet starts an argument. He insists that al-Iklil, the lunar mansion called "the Crown", is a group of three dim stars near the balance. He calls those who identify it with the Scorpion's forehead plainly mistaken, and uses the Moon's path to prove his point.

stories.title: A bigger Scorpion
stories.text: The Greeks gave Libra its own balance, but the Arabs saw its two bright stars as the claws of the Scorpion. Zubana means the claws or "pincers", so their scorpion was much bigger than the modern one. The old saying for their rising in late autumn: "When al-Zubana rise, they bring every family man a worry and every herd-owner a hardship, and people say 'there was this and there was that': so gather in for your family, and do not delay." In other words, the cold has arrived.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); Commentary on the site (Abha al-Mawakib)

full.e: After it come the stars of the Balance; among them al-Zubana, two stars,
both lustrous and flashing, a lance-length apart;
together they are the two pans of the Balance, and they are known as the Scorpion's hand,
and they were also named the Zubana of summer, when al-Butayn sets as they rise.
They are followed by al-Iklil, the Crown, three stars, all of them dim:
one of them a star of the Balance, far from the point where the tongue of the scale is fixed,
and a star among those left out of the figure of the Balance when it was observed,
and a star above them that was not observed, not far from those that were.
The reporters disagreed about al-Iklil, and all of them wander in error,
for they took it to be the stars that most of the reporters know
as the Forehead of the Scorpion: three stars like blazing meteors.
But the ignorance of whoever claims this is clear, because al-Zubana are far from them,

a: إن فارق الكفّة في السير قصر
full.e: while the Heart is close to them; so if the Moon, leaving the pan of the scale, fell short
in its course of reaching the Forehead, and likewise if it travelled on and turned its face
from the Scorpion's Forehead toward its Heart, it would pass it, because it is so close
to the star of the Heart we mentioned. So al-Iklil is nothing but what we have said.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 16 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الميزان. نجماه النيّران بينهما قيد رمح هما الزُّبانى، كفّتا الميزان ويدا العقرب، ويسمّيان زبانى الصيف. ثم يدخل الناظم في جدال: يصرّ على أن الإكليل (منزل القمر) ثلاثة كواكب خافتة قرب الميزان، ويرى أن من جعله جبهة العقرب مخطئ خطأً واضحًا، ويحتجّ بمسير القمر.

stories.title: عقرب أكبر
stories.text: جعل الإغريق للميزان كوكبة مستقلة، أما العرب فرأوا نجميه النيّرين زُبانَيْ العقرب، أي قرنيها أو كلّابيها، فكانت عقربهم أكبر من العقرب الحديثة. وسجع طلوعهما في آخر الخريف: «إذا طلعت الزبانى، أحدثت لكل ذي عيال شأنًا، ولكل ذي ماشية هوانًا، وقالوا كان وكانا، فاجمع لأهلك ولا تَوانى»، أي قد هجم البرد.

greek.seen: The scales of justice (once, the scorpion's claws).

stories.title: The claws that became scales
stories.text: For the early Greeks these stars were Chelae, the claws of the Scorpion, just as they were for the Arabs (al-Zubana). The Romans later made them a separate constellation, the scales, and linked them to Astraea, goddess of justice (Virgo), who holds them beside her.
stories.source: Ptolemy, Almagest; Manilius, Astronomica

ar.seen: ميزان العدل (وكان من قبل كلّابي العقرب).

stories.title: الكلّابان اللذان صارا ميزانًا
stories.text: كانت هذه النجوم عند أقدم الإغريق «كيلاي» أي كلّابي العقرب، كما كانت عند العرب «الزبانى». ثم جعلها الرومان كوكبة مستقلة هي الميزان، وربطوها بأستريا إلهة العدل (العذراء) تمسكه بجانبها.

arab.seen: Scorpius, whose bright stars "some call the Lion of Winter". Its great red star, "like a live coal", is Qalb al-'Aqrab, the Scorpion's Heart (Antares), and it appears in Arab poems and speeches. Stars on either side are al-Niyat, the arteries. The two stars of the sting are al-Shawla, the raised tail. The Heart and the Falling Eagle (Vega), rising together, are called al-Harraran, "the two growlers".

stories.title: The two growlers of winter
stories.text: The Heart of the Scorpion and the Falling Eagle rise together on cold mornings, and the Arabs called them al-Harraran, "the two that growl". Ibn Qutayba explains that winter was compared to a snarling dog, and these stars rise "with the growling of winter". The Scorpion was also ill-omened: the Arabs disliked starting a journey while the Moon was in it. The rhymed saying for its rising: "When the Scorpion rises, the water freezes in the gullies, the grey-haired man draws near the fire, the locust dies, and the akhtab bird falls silent."
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: After it come the stars of the Scorpion, stars shining in the darkness,
their bodies blooming and bright; the ancients named them the Figure;
it is also called the Lion of Winter, in most lands and among most tribes;
all the Bedouins and the non-Arabs know it; among them is a star like a blazing meteor;
brilliant light rises over it, with a redness, as if when it blazes it were a live coal;
the Bedouins named it the Heart of the Scorpion; it comes up in their poems and their speeches.
It is followed by one star and comes after another, both lustrous, which are called
by the Bedouins the Arteries, know it; it is followed by a small, dim star,
going before a shining, ill-omened star, a hand-span apart when measured;
the Greeks and the experts make them the sting of the Scorpion's figure,
and one whose word I do not reject told me they are called al-Shawla, the raised tail.
And the Heart, together with a bright, gleaming star that the Arabs know as the Falling Eagle,
are both called the Two Growlers, in most times and most lands.
We have already described the state of the Forehead, summarised, leaving no doubt.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 14 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: العقرب، ونجومها المضيئة «تسمّى أسد الشتاء». نجمها الأحمر العظيم «كأنه جمرة» هو قلب العقرب ويرد في أشعار العرب وخطبهم. والنجمان على جانبيه هما النِّياط، ونجما الإبرة هما الشَّولة أي الذنب المرفوع. والقلب مع النسر الواقع يطلعان معًا ويسمّيان الهرّاران.

stories.title: هرّارا الشتاء
stories.text: يطلع قلب العقرب والنسر الواقع معًا في صباحات البرد فسمّتهما العرب «الهرّارين». ويشرح ابن قتيبة أنهم شبّهوا الشتاء بالكلب، وأن هذين يطلعان «لهرير الشتاء عند طلوعهما». وكانت العقرب مشؤومة عندهم فكرهوا السفر والقمر نازل بها. وسجع طلوعها: «إذا طلعت العقرب، جَمَس المِذنب، وقَرُب الأشيب، ومات الجُندب، ولم يَصِرّ الأخطب».

greek.seen: The scorpion that killed Orion.

stories.title: Orion and the scorpion
stories.text: The hunter Orion boasted that he would kill every animal on earth. The Earth goddess Gaia (or Artemis, in some versions) sent a giant scorpion, which stung him to death. Both were placed in the sky, but on opposite sides, so that when the Scorpion rises in the east, Orion sets in the west, still fleeing from it.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia; Ovid, Fasti 5

ar.seen: العقرب التي قتلت أوريون.

stories.title: أوريون والعقرب
stories.text: تباهى الصيّاد أوريون بأنه سيقتل كل حيوان على الأرض، فأرسلت إلهة الأرض غايا (أو أرتميس في روايات) عقربًا عظيمة لدغته فمات. ورُفع الاثنان إلى السماء لكن في جهتين متقابلتين، فإذا طلعت العقرب في الشرق غرب أوريون في الغرب كأنه ما زال يفرّ منها.

china.seen: The Azure Dragon of the East; Antares is Shang, the 'Great Fire'.

stories.title: The dragon's heart
stories.text: Scorpius forms the heart and tail of Qinglong, the Azure Dragon, guardian of the eastern sky and of spring. Its red star Antares was called Dahuo, the Great Fire, or Xin, the Heart. Its position marked the seasons for farmers. In the 'Shen and Shang' story it is the star Shang, which never meets its brother Shen (Orion).
stories.source: Shiji; Zuo zhuan

poem.orig:
人生不相见，动如参与商。
今夕复何夕，共此灯烛光。
poem.trans:
In this life, friends do not meet; they move like Shen and Shang.
What night is this, then, that we share this candle's light?
poem.by: Du Fu, 'To My Retired Friend Wei' (759)

ar.seen: التنين الأزرق حارس الشرق، وقلب العقرب هو «شانغ» أي «النار العظيمة».

stories.title: قلب التنين
stories.text: تكوّن العقرب قلب «تشينغلونغ» التنين الأزرق وذيله، حارس السماء الشرقية وحارس الربيع. وكان قلب العقرب الأحمر يسمّى «داهوو» أي النار العظيمة، أو «شين» أي القلب، وكان موضعه يدلّ الفلاحين على المواسم. وهو في حكاية «شِن وشانغ» نجم شانغ الذي لا يلقى أخاه شِن (الجبّار) أبدًا.

stories.title: The fishing hook
stories.text: In fishing villages around the Seto Inland Sea, the curved tail of Scorpius was Uo-tsuri-boshi, 'the fish-catching star', or Tai-tsuri-boshi, the hook for catching sea bream. It hangs low over the southern sea on summer nights.
stories.source: Japanese star folklore collected by Nojiri Hōei

ar.seen: أوو-تسوري-بوشي، نجم صنّارة الصيد.

stories.title: صنّارة الصيد
stories.text: في قرى الصيد حول بحر سيتو الداخلي كان ذيل العقرب المقوّس «أوو-تسوري-بوشي» أي نجم صيد السمك، أو «تاي-تسوري-بوشي» صنّارة صيد سمك الدنيس. وهو يتدلّى منخفضًا فوق البحر الجنوبي في ليالي الصيف.

india.seen: Jyeshtha, 'the eldest' (Antares), and the scorpion Vrishchika.

stories.title: The eldest
stories.text: Antares is Jyeshtha, 'the eldest', ruled by Indra, king of the gods. The stars around it form Anuradha and Mula ('the root'), lunar mansions of the scorpion, Vrishchika.
stories.source: Wikipedia, 'Jyeshtha'

ar.seen: جيشتا، «الكبرى» (قلب العقرب)، والعقرب فريشتشيكا.

stories.title: الكبرى
stories.text: قلب العقرب هو «جيشتا» أي الكبرى، ويحكمها إندرا ملك الآلهة. والنجوم حوله تكوّن «أنورادها» و«مولا» أي الجذر، وهي منازل العقرب «فريشتشيكا».

safrica.seen: !Xu San: Antares is the 'fire-finishing star'. Khoikhoi: the eyes of the lion.

stories.title: When the fires die down
stories.text: The !Xu San call Antares the 'fire-finishing star', because it is seen late at night when the campfires burn down to embers. The Khoikhoi called two stars of the Scorpion's tail (Mu-1 and Mu-2) xami di mura, 'the eyes of the lion'.
stories.source: Astronomical Society of Southern Africa, 'African Ethnoastronomy' (after P. G. Alcock, Venus Rising, 2014)

af.seen: !Xu San: Antares is die 'vuur-klaarmaak-ster'. Khoikhoi: die oë van die leeu.

stories.title: Wanneer die vure doodgaan
stories.text: Die !Xu San noem Antares die 'vuur-klaarmaak-ster', omdat hy laat in die nag gesien word, wanneer die kampvure tot kole uitgebrand het. Die Khoikhoi het twee sterre in die Skerpioen se stert (Mu-1 en Mu-2) xami di mura genoem, 'die oë van die leeu'.

ar.seen: سان !زو: قلب العقرب «النجم الذي يُنهي النار». الخويخوي: عينا الأسد.

stories.title: حين تخبو النيران
stories.text: يسمّي سان !زو قلب العقرب «النجم الذي يُنهي النار» لأنه يُرى في آخر الليل حين تخبو نيران المخيّم فتصير جمرًا. وسمّى الخويخوي نجمين في ذيل العقرب (مو-1 ومو-2) «خامي دي مورا» أي عينا الأسد.

arab.seen: Sagittarius, "the Bow" or "the Archer". The Arabs saw ostriches here. A curve of stars like a cloud, which the Greeks made the archer's flying head-cloth, is al-Udhi, the ostrich nest, also called al-Qilada, the necklace. Four bright stars are al-Na'am al-Sadir, ostriches returning from water, and four before them are al-Na'am al-Warid, ostriches going down to drink. The space between is al-Wasl. Two stars on the bow are al-Zalimān, the two male ostriches. There are also al-Suradan (two shrikes), al-Bayd (the eggs), al-Yamamatan (two doves) and al-Qata (sandgrouse). An empty patch "like a bare desert" is al-Balda.

stories.title: The ostriches at the river
stories.text: The Milky Way is thickest in Sagittarius, and the Arabs saw it as a river with a flock of ostriches drinking. Ibn Qutayba writes: "Al-Na'a'im are eight stars. Four are in the Milky Way: the Ostriches Going Down, called so because they have entered the water. Four are outside it: the Ostriches Coming Back, as if they had drunk and turned away." Around them is the whole ostrich family: the two males (al-Zalimān), the chicks (al-Ri'al), the eggs and the round nest scraped in the sand (al-Udhi). Just beyond is al-Balda, an empty stretch of sky with no stars at all. Al-Ma'arri's line, "who created the ostriches in their haunts", plays on these sky-ostriches.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); Kitab al-Sama'

full.e: After it comes the Bow, also called the Archer: stars that shine in the dark;
among them stars like a cloud strung in a row, which the Greeks make the Archer's head-cloth;
they are known as the Nest and the Necklace; beneath them are blazing stars,
four that dazzle the eye, known as the Returning Ostriches;
in front of them are bright stars that resemble them within the figure,
most like ostriches running wild: they named them the Ostriches Going Down to Water.
Between the two flocks of ostriches you see an open space, which the desert Arabs call al-Wasl, the Link.
On the curved tip of the Archer's bow you see two stars like the stars of the ostriches;
they are raised above al-Wasl, and they are called the Two Male Ostriches.
Among the stars of the Bow are two stars, both on the horse's thigh;
the Arabs call them the Two Shrikes; around them are blazing stars
which the scholars named the Eggs, and we have also heard them called the Shells.
Around them are stars gathered together, small, four in number;
from them the tail begins toward the end: the Arabs named them the Two Doves.
Between them and the star of the Frog, which is at the end of the Bucket's stream,
are stars strung together and intertwined, and among them, from the stars of the Fish,
on its side, its chest and its back, are stars the Bedouins also know as the Sandgrouse,
near the stars of the Eggs and the Nest, and the region likened to the western sphere.
A little patch like an empty desert, bare: the learned named it al-Balda.
And the stars strung together and standing out they call the Young She-Camels.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 20 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: القوس أو الرامي. ورأى العرب هنا نعامًا: نجوم مقوّسة كالسحاب جعلها الروم عذبة الرامي هي الأُدحيّ أي عشّ النعام، وتسمّى القلادة. وأربعة كواكب نيّرة هي النعام الصادر الراجع من الماء، وأربعة أمامها هي النعام الوارد. والفضاء بينهما الوَصل. ونجمان على القوس هما الظليمان أي ذكرا النعام، وفيها الصُّرَدان والبَيض واليمامتان والقطا، وبقعة جرداء «كالفلاة» هي البلدة.

stories.title: النعام عند النهر
stories.text: المجرة أكثف ما تكون في القوس، فرآها العرب نهرًا يرده سرب من النعام. قال ابن قتيبة: «النعائم ثمانية كواكب، أربعة في المجرة وهي النعام الوارد، سُمّي واردًا لأنه شرع في المجرة، وأربعة خارجة عن المجرة وهي النعام الصادر، كأنه شرب ثم صدر». وحولها أسرة النعام كلها: الظليمان، والرِّئال (الفراخ)، والبيض، والأُدحيّ المستدير في الرمل. وبعدها «البلدة» رقعة خالية لا كواكب فيها. وقول المعرّي «ومن برأ النعائم في حراها» يلمّح إلى نعائم السماء هذه.

greek.seen: A centaur archer: Crotus, or Chiron.

stories.title: The archer
stories.text: Eratosthenes said the Archer is Crotus, son of Pan, who lived among the Muses on Mount Helicon, invented archery, and first applauded their songs by clapping. The Muses asked Zeus to place him among the stars. Later writers saw him as a centaur, half man and half horse, aiming his arrow at the heart of the Scorpion. Heracles fought the violent centaurs.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia; Kitab al-Sama'

ar.seen: قنطور رامٍ: كروتوس أو خيرون.

stories.title: الرامي
stories.text: قال إراتوستينس إن الرامي هو كروتوس ابن بان، عاش بين ربّات الفنون على جبل هيليكون، واخترع الرماية، وكان أول من صفّق لأغانيهن، فطلبت ربّات الفنون من زيوس أن يرفعه بين النجوم. ورآه الكتّاب المتأخرون قنطورًا نصفه إنسان ونصفه حصان يصوّب سهمه نحو قلب العقرب. وقد قاتل هرقل القناطير العنيفة.

china.seen: Nandou, the Southern Dipper, which keeps the records of life.

stories.title: The keeper of births
stories.text: Six stars of Sagittarius (our 'Teapot' handle and lid) make the Southern Dipper. 'The Southern Dipper records life, the Northern Dipper records death,' people said. In the Soushen ji story (see Ursa Major), the Southern Dipper is the old man who lengthens a young man's life from nineteen years to ninety-nine.
stories.source: Gan Bao, Soushen ji

ar.seen: ناندو، المغرفة الجنوبية التي تسجّل الأعمار.

stories.title: كاتب المواليد
stories.text: ستة نجوم من القوس (يد «إبريق الشاي» وغطاؤه) تكوّن المغرفة الجنوبية. وكان الناس يقولون: «المغرفة الجنوبية تسجّل الحياة، والمغرفة الشمالية تسجّل الموت». وفي حكاية «سوشن جي» (انظر الدب الأكبر) المغرفة الجنوبية هي الشيخ الذي مدّ عمر الشاب من تسع عشرة سنة إلى تسع وتسعين.

arab.seen: Capricornus, the Kid (goat). Two stars on its horns, with a tiny star almost touching one of them, look "like a smiling mouth with glistening teeth". The Arabs called them Sa'd al-Dhabih, "the luck of the slaughterer". Next come Sa'd Bula' and, among bright stars in the figure, Sa'd Nashira. Someone reported that these two are also called "the two lovers".

stories.title: The slaughterer and his sheep
stories.text: Sa'd al-Dhabih is two stars, with a third tiny one pressed against the upper star. The Bedouins said the tiny star is "his sheep, which he is slaughtering". That's where the name "Luck of the Slaughterer" comes from. It rose at dawn in the deep cold of January, just as Suhail rose at sunset, and the young camels moved up to a new age. The saying for it: "When Sa'd al-Dhabih rises, the barking dog guards his people, the man who returns at evening brings them firewood, and the herdsman lies in late." It was too cold to take the flocks out early.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); al-Marzuqi, al-Azmina wa al-Amkina (11th c.)

full.e: After mentioning the stars of the Archer, I describe the shape of the Kid in my words:
stars blooming in the darkness, known to every nation as the Kid.
On its two horns you see two stars, and just below the brighter of the two
a little star whose glow catches the eye, almost touching the larger one:
it is like a smiling mouth with gleaming teeth; the Arabs call it the Luck of the Slaughterer.
It is followed by two stars with a glittering light, which the Bedouins call Sa'd Bula', the Luck of the Swallower.
Within the figure are two stars which appear when the Slaughterer appears,
both brilliant, flashing as they twinkle, adorned by a body of pure white light;
around them are bright stars, which the Arabs call Sa'd Nashira;
and one who reports from the Arabs told that 'the Two Lovers' is a name for these two.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 10 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الجدي. نجمان على قرنيه وكويكب يكاد يلتصق بأحدهما «كأنها مباسم ذات شَنَب»، تسمّيها العرب سعد الذابح. ويتبعه سعد بُلَع، ومن نجومه النيّرة سعد ناشرة. وروى بعضهم أن «المحبّين» لقب لهذين.

stories.title: الذابح وشاته
stories.text: سعد الذابح كوكبان وبقرب الأعلى منهما كوكب صغير يكاد يلزق به، قالت الأعراب: هو «شاته التي يذبحها»، ومن هنا اسمه. وكان يطلع فجرًا في شدة برد يناير، ويطلع سهيل حينئذ مع المغرب، وتنتقل أسنان الإبل. وسجعه: «إذا طلع سعد الذابح، حمى أهلَه النابح، ونفع أهلَه الرائح، وتصبّح السارح»، أي لزم الكلب أهله، وجاء الرائح بالحطب، وتأخّر الراعي في الغدوّ لشدة البرد.

greek.seen: A goat with a fish's tail: the god Pan.

stories.title: Pan escapes the monster
stories.text: When the terrible monster Typhon attacked the gods, they fled in fear and changed into animals. The god Pan leapt into the Nile and began to turn into a fish, but only his lower half changed. He ended up half goat and half fish. Zeus placed that strange shape in the sky. Another story says it is Amalthea, the goat who nursed baby Zeus.
stories.source: Hyginus, De Astronomia; Ovid, Metamorphoses 5

ar.seen: جدي بذيل سمكة: الإله بان.

stories.title: بان يفرّ من الوحش
stories.text: لمّا هاجم الوحش المريع تيفون الآلهة فرّوا خائفين وتحوّلوا حيوانات. فقفز الإله بان في النيل وبدأ يتحوّل سمكة، لكن نصفه الأسفل وحده تحوّل، فصار نصفه جديًا ونصفه سمكة، فوضع زيوس هذه الصورة الغريبة في السماء. وتقول رواية أخرى إنه أمالثيا العنز التي أرضعت زيوس.

arab.seen: Aquarius, "the Bucket" or "the Water-Pourer". The commentary points out that these names are translations from Greek. The stars are pictured as a man holding a full bucket in his right hand, pouring out water that runs south "like a river". It ends at a brilliant star the Arabs call al-Difdi' al-Awwal, "the First Frog" (Fomalhaut), which the Greeks make the mouth of the Southern Fish. Then come the lucky stars: Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud ("the luck of lucks"), Sa'd al-Malik, and Sa'd al-Akhbiya, "the luck of the tents", whose rising signals pleasant weather.

stories.title: The swallower
stories.text: Sa'd Bula' is two stars, one of them very faint. Ibn Qutayba says it was called Bula', "the swallower", "because it swallowed the other, faint one, and took its light". Al-Marzuqi records another explanation he didn't believe: that it rose at the moment God said to the earth after Noah's flood, "O earth, swallow your water!" (Quran 11:44).
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.); al-Marzuqi, al-Azmina wa al-Amkina (11th c.)

stories.title: The luck of lucks, and the luck of the tents
stories.text: Sa'd al-Su'ud rose in February, when the hard winter finally softened, so it was the luckiest of all: "When Sa'd al-Su'ud rises, the branches turn green, the skins grow soft, everything frozen melts, and people no longer like to sit in the sun." Sa'd al-Akhbiya is one bright star with three around it, which some said are its "tents". Ibn Qutayba prefers another reason for the name: it rises just as the warm season begins, "and the crawling creatures that were hidden come out" from their winter hiding-places.
stories.source: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-Anwa' (9th c.)

full.e: After it we explain the shape of the Bucket-carrier, summarised in the briefest words.
It is what the Arabs call the Bucket, and the Water-Pourer is another of its names.

a: في يده اليمنى ذنوب قد ملي
full.e: Stars likened to a man holding in his right hand a full bucket,
pouring out waters from the bucket that stretch like a river to the south;
they end at a brilliant star, adorned with light that dazzles the eyes,
shining like the moon when the moon sets: the Arabs call it the First Frog.
The early Greeks, and those who study the stars, make it the mouth of the Fish, know this;
and sometimes it is called the Male Ostrich; and it is the one that the Greeks make
the mouth of the figure of the Southern Fish, as those who follow the astrologers claim.
Yes, and within this figure are three small stars;

a: هي من الصورة في بطن اليد
full.e: in the figure they are on the palm of the hand; the Arabs make them one of the Lucky Stars;

a: تبدو من الأفق إذا الجدي طلع
وهي التي قد لقبت سعد بلع
full.e: they appear on the horizon when the Kid rises, and they are the ones named Sa'd Bula'.
They are followed by two stars, close to one another;
the higher of the two is like a burning ember: the Arabs call them the Luck of Lucks.
They are followed by two other stars, two hand-spans or two finger-spans apart;

a: خبر من في علمه لم يرتبك
full.e: one who is not confused in his knowledge told that they were named Sa'd al-Malik, the Luck of the King.
They lie on the shoulder of this figure, followed by bright stars,
three, surrounding one star, and all of them large stars;
their rising is a sign of fine weather: the Arabs named them the Luck of the Tents.
They are far from the Milky Way, which is called the Stars of the Trail.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 20 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الدلو أو ساكب الماء، ويذكر الشرح أن الاسمين مترجمان عن اليونانية. صُوّرت نجومه برجل في يده اليمنى ذَنوب مملوء يسكب منه ماء يمتد «كالنهر إلى الجنوب»، وينقطع عند نجم ساطع تسمّيه العرب الضفدع الأول ويجعله الروم فم الحوت الجنوبي. ثم السعود: سعد بُلَع وسعد السعود وسعد الملك وسعد الأخبية الذي يدل طلوعه على طيب الهواء.

stories.title: البالع
stories.text: سعد بلع نجمان أحدهما خفيّ جدًا، قال ابن قتيبة: سُمّي بالعًا «لأنه كان بلع الآخر الخفيّ وأخذ ضوءه». وذكر المرزوقي قولًا آخر لم يرتضه: أنه سُمّي بلعًا لأنه طلع حين قيل ﴿يا أرضُ ابلعي ماءك﴾ بعد الطوفان.

stories.title: سعد السعود وسعد الأخبية
stories.text: يطلع سعد السعود في فبراير حين يلين الشتاء أخيرًا، فكان أيمن السعود: «إذا طلع سعد السعود، نَضَر العود، ولانت الجلود، وذاب كلّ مجمود، وكُره الناس في الشمس القعود». وسعد الأخبية كوكب نيّر حوله ثلاثة قيل إنها أخبيته، ويرجّح ابن قتيبة سببًا آخر للاسم: أنه يطلع في قُبُل الدفء «فيخرج من الهوامّ ما كان مختبئًا».

greek.seen: A youth pouring water: Ganymede.

stories.title: The cup-bearer of the gods
stories.text: Ganymede was a Trojan prince of great beauty. Zeus's eagle (Aquila) carried him off to Olympus, where he became the cup-bearer of the gods, pouring nectar at their feasts. In the sky he pours an endless stream from his jar, and it flows down into the mouth of the Southern Fish.
stories.source: Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi; Hyginus, De Astronomia

ar.seen: فتى يسكب الماء: غانيميد.

stories.title: ساقي الآلهة
stories.text: كان غانيميد أميرًا طرواديًا بارع الجمال، فحمله نسر زيوس (العقاب) إلى الأولمب ليكون ساقي الآلهة يصبّ لهم الرحيق في ولائمهم. وهو في السماء يسكب من جرّته سيلًا لا ينقطع يجري إلى فم الحوت الجنوبي.

arab.seen: Pisces, also called al-Samaka, the Fish: tangled stars that the Greeks likened to two little fishes, one close to Andromeda. Cloud-like stars joining them are al-Wasl, "the link". With this the poet closes the twelve signs of the zodiac and turns to the southern sky.

stories.title: When the Fish rises
stories.text: The bright star Batn al-Hut, "the belly of the fish" (in Andromeda), rising before dawn meant the equinox had come. The Arabs said: "When the Fish rises, the nets are set, travel becomes easy, thorns cling to the clothes, and the season is pleasant for the hermits." Bird-catchers spread their nets because birds were migrating, and the desert thorns caught on people's clothes.
stories.source: Kitab al-Sama'

full.e: Then comes the Fish, also called the Samaka: stars tangled and intertwined;
the Greeks likened them to two fishes, which the eye sees as small.
One of them comes close to the Chained Woman, with joined stars between them,
strung like a cloud, known among the Bedouins as al-Wasl, the Link.
Now we have mentioned the figures of the zodiac, and here we begin to go out
to the stars of the southern figures, and mention them all in order.

poem.by: Ibn al-Sufi, Urjuzat al-Kawakib (around 1000 CE), all 6 couplets for this constellation

ar.seen: الحوت، ويسمّى السمكة: نجوم ملتفّة شبّهها الروم بنونين صغيرتين، إحداهما قرب المرأة المسلسلة، وبينهما نجوم كالسحاب هي الوَصل. وبه يختم الناظم البروج الاثني عشر وينتقل إلى السماء الجنوبية.

stories.title: إذا طلعت السمكة
stories.text: كان طلوع «بطن الحوت» قبيل الشروق علامة على الاعتدال، فقالت العرب: «إذا طلعت السمكة، نُصبت الشبكة، وأمكنت الحركة، وتعلّقت بالثوب الحَسَكة، وطاب الزمان للنَّسَكة»: يُنصب صائدو الطير شباكهم لنزول الطير، ويتعلّق شوك نبات الصحراء بالثياب، ويطيب الجو للنسّاك السائحين.

greek.seen: Two fish tied together by a cord: Aphrodite and Eros.

stories.title: The fish tied together
stories.text: When the monster Typhon attacked the gods, Aphrodite and her son Eros fled to the river Euphrates and turned into fish to escape. They tied themselves together with a cord so they would not lose each other in the water. The two fish and the cord between them were placed in the sky.
stories.source: Hyginus; Ovid, Fasti 2

ar.seen: سمكتان مربوطتان بحبل: أفروديت وإيروس.

stories.title: السمكتان المربوطتان
stories.text: لمّا هاجم الوحش تيفون الآلهة فرّت أفروديت وابنها إيروس إلى نهر الفرات وتحوّلا سمكتين لينجوا، وربطا نفسيهما بحبل كي لا يضيع أحدهما من الآخر في الماء. فوُضعت السمكتان والحبل بينهما في السماء.

arab.seen: Cetus, the first southern figure: a sea monster with the face of a lion and the tail of a dolphin, which the Greeks and "everyone connected with the stars" called Qitus. Together with part of the River, the Arabs call its stars al-Baqar, the cows. A star on its snout is al-Kaff al-Jadhma', "the cut-off hand" of al-Thurayya. Four stars in a broad square are al-Na'amat, the ostriches. A star at the root of the tail is al-Difdi' al-Thani, "the Second Frog" (Diphda), also called the herdsman of the ostriches. Four faint stars between are al-Nizam, "the string of beads".

stories.title: Al-Thurayya's shorter hand
stories.text: Al-Thurayya's two arms reach out in opposite directions. Her long right arm reaches north to Cassiopeia, where her hand is painted with henna. Her left arm is short and runs south under Aries to end here, on the sea monster's head. That is al-Kaff al-Jadhma', "the cut-off hand", as if it had been severed. A poet describes her at setting time, "stretching out her cut-off hand a little, like one hoping to clasp the hand of the beloved."
